about: A toolkit for taking programs apart to study how they work, used by security researchers.

prs.title: x86 multiply instructions now assemble to the right bytes
prs.broken: The built-in x86 assembler wrote the wrong bytes for most multiply instructions with two or three operands. It used the wrong registers for the newer ones and the wrong length for many constants, with no error.
prs.changed: Multiply now uses the same careful encoder as the move instructions. Nearly every one of 2373 tested forms matches GNU's assembler, up from 569, and impossible ones are refused.
prs.matters: Patches with a multiply in them do what was typed, instead of silently corrupting the program.

prs.title: x86 math with a constant now assembles to the right bytes
prs.broken: For eight basic math and compare instructions with a constant, the built-in x86 assembler often wrote the wrong bytes without any error, for example using a different register than the one written.
prs.changed: These instructions now use the same encoder as the shift instructions. All 3600 tested 64-bit forms match GNU's assembler, up from 3096, and constants too big for the operand are refused.
prs.matters: Patches written in radare2 run the instruction that was typed, not a silently different one.

prs.title: The x86 assembler can write the instruction the disassembler shows
prs.broken: radare2 shows one common 64-bit sign-extend instruction under a name its own built-in assembler did not know. Copying a disassembled line back to patch it failed with an error.
prs.changed: The assembler now writes that instruction for every register and memory form, and accepts the other common spelling too. All 176 forms were checked against GNU's assembler.
prs.matters: People patching 64-bit programs can write back exactly what radare2 showed them.

prs.title: The arm64 assembler keeps the condition you wrote
prs.broken: For three conditional instructions, the arm64 assembler only recognised the equal condition and turned every other one, like less-than or higher, into not-equal. The code it produced did something different from what was written.
prs.changed: The assembler now reads every condition name and encodes it, and refuses names it does not know instead of guessing.
prs.matters: Patching or writing arm64 code in radare2 gives the instruction that was asked for.

prs.title: radiff2 now shows the real file names in its unified diff
prs.broken: When you compared two files as a unified diff, the header showed the names of hidden temporary files instead of the files you gave it.
prs.changed: The diff now labels each side with the name you passed in. Other tools that use the same diff code behave as before.
prs.matters: The output reads like a normal diff, so you can tell which side is which and feed it to other tools.

prs.title: The fletcher64 checksum now matches other tools
prs.broken: radare2 let the running sums of its fletcher64 checksum wrap around instead of reducing them the way the algorithm says, so anything longer than a few bytes got a different checksum than other tools give.
prs.changed: The sums are now reduced after every word, the same way the 32-bit version already worked.
prs.matters: A fletcher64 checksum from radare2 can be compared with one from any other tool.

prs.title: The 64-bit assembler now writes address calculations correctly
prs.broken: In 64-bit mode, the instruction that computes an address dropped the index register, its scale, the extra registers and the operand size, so the assembled code computed a different address.
prs.changed: It now goes through the same encoder as the memory moves fixed just before it, and matches the GNU assembler on 175 tested forms.
prs.matters: Address calculations written inside radare2 assemble to what was typed.

prs.title: The 64-bit assembler now writes the right memory moves
prs.broken: In 64-bit mode, the built-in assembler turned many instructions that move data between a register and memory into a different instruction, or refused them. A load could use the wrong register, drop part of the address, or fail outright.
prs.changed: Loads and stores that use an address register now go through one encoder that builds every part of the instruction the way the GNU assembler does. Over 1,400 tested forms now match it.
prs.matters: Code written or patched inside radare2 does what it says.

prs.title: Two file hashes no longer depend on the computer's byte order
prs.broken: The elf and xorpair hashes read and wrote their data in whatever byte order the computer used, so they could give different results on different machines.
prs.changed: Both now use a fixed byte order. Results on common PCs are unchanged.
prs.matters: The same file gives the same hash on any machine.

prs.title: The DEX checksum fix macro now writes a valid checksum
prs.broken: When a DEX file's checksum was wrong, the tool suggested a fix that wrote the checksum in the wrong byte order, so the file stayed broken.
prs.changed: The adler32 hash command now prints its bytes in the same order as the rahash2 tool, and tests cover both the hash and the fix.
prs.matters: The suggested fix now repairs the file.

prs.title: Struct views now color addresses by what they point to
prs.broken: The toolkit can lay out memory as a struct, field by field. Fields holding addresses were printed as plain numbers, so you could not tell code from data at a glance, unlike its other memory views.
prs.changed: With colors on, those fields are now colored by the kind of memory they point to: code, writable data or read-only data. Plain and machine-readable output stay the same.
prs.matters: Pointers to code or writable memory stand out while reading a struct.

prs.title: File fingerprints now match the standard ssdeep tool
prs.broken: The toolkit can make a fuzzy fingerprint of a file, used to spot near-copies of malware. Its fingerprints differed from the standard ssdeep tool for many files, and small files got none at all.
prs.changed: The fingerprint is now worked out the same way the standard tool does it, with a fresh start on each pass and the same minimum size.
prs.matters: Researchers can compare the toolkit's fingerprints with ones made anywhere else.

prs.title: The search tool no longer crashes on a badly written pattern
prs.broken: The toolkit's search tool takes patterns written between slashes. Without the slashes, the release version crashed and newer builds silently skipped that search.
prs.changed: The tool now says the pattern is invalid and how to write it, and still runs the other searches.
prs.matters: Users get a clear message instead of a crash or quietly missing results.

prs.title: The hash tool now prints entropy in every output mode
prs.broken: The toolkit's hash tool can measure a file's entropy, a sign of whether data is packed or encrypted. In quiet, JSON and some other modes it printed nothing, or random bytes from memory, instead of the number.
prs.changed: Every output mode now uses one shared step for entropy and the other special cases.
prs.matters: Scripts that ask for entropy in JSON or quiet mode get the real number.

prs.title: The hash tool's JSON mode works for files again
prs.broken: Asking the hash tool for one JSON object per file printed only the file name and nothing else.
prs.changed: The JSON object is now printed for files, the same as for text given on the command line.
prs.matters: Scripts that read the tool's JSON output get the hashes they asked for.

prs.title: The number converter shows the right old-style address
prs.broken: The toolkit's number converter also shows an address in the split format early PCs used. It dropped part of the number, so it showed a different address than the main tool did.
prs.changed: It now uses the same calculation as the main tool.
prs.matters: Both parts of the toolkit agree, and the address shown is the right one.

prs.title: Negative numbers now work with every option of the number converter
prs.broken: Giving the number converter a negative number, like -1, made it ignore the option you asked for, such as decimal output or a size like 'g' for gigabytes, and just print hex.
prs.changed: Negative numbers now go through the same steps as positive ones.
prs.matters: Converting -1 to decimal gives -1, not a long hex number.

prs.title: The number converter now reads every line it is given
prs.broken: Piping several numbers into the number converter, one per line, converted only the first. The line break at the end also confused it, so '1f' came out as 1.
prs.changed: Each line is now cleaned up and converted on its own, as if it were typed separately.
prs.matters: Scripts can feed a whole list of numbers through the converter in one go.

prs.title: Inserting bytes into a file no longer cuts off its end
prs.broken: radare2 lets you insert bytes into a file and push the rest along. With the default settings, the last few bytes fell off the end and were replaced by zeros.
prs.changed: I made the insert move the rest of the file directly, so nothing is lost at the end.
prs.matters: Editing a file this way no longer silently damages it.

prs.title: The file comparison tool shows every change
prs.broken: radare2's tool for comparing two files skipped changes of a single byte, could print random memory for some inputs, and in one mode stopped after the first change.
prs.changed: I fixed how it copies the changed bytes, made it stop reading at the right place, and let it carry on past the first change.
prs.matters: A comparison now lists every difference between the two files, and only what is really there.

prs.title: The assembler's word view shows bytes in the right order
prs.broken: radare2's assembler can print machine code as 4-byte words. For big-endian targets the bytes came out reversed, long output never wrapped, and a short result read past the end of its memory.
prs.changed: I made it read words in the target's byte order, pad the last partial word, and start a new line every eight words.
prs.matters: The word view now matches the real bytes for any target, and short inputs no longer read stray memory.

prs.title: rafind2 reports every match, even back-to-back ones
prs.broken: When a pattern appeared twice in a row, like a run of repeated bytes, rafind2 only reported the first match and dropped the next one with a warning. The r2 search command found them all.
prs.changed: I made rafind2 accept matches that start right where the previous one ended, the same as r2's own search.
prs.matters: A search through a binary no longer hides real hits in repeated data.

prs.title: rahash2 can hash empty files
prs.broken: rahash2 refused any empty file with "Invalid file size", for every hash type, while other tools give the standard hash of empty input.
prs.changed: I made empty files get the same hash as empty input for every algorithm; only a byte range that cannot fit still errors.
prs.matters: Hashing a folder of files no longer fails on the empty ones.

prs.title: rahash2 hashes the same range of every file
prs.broken: When hashing several files with a byte range, rahash2 used that range only for the first file and hashed the rest to the end, so their hashes were wrong.
prs.changed: I made each file get the range that was asked for, while files without a range still use their full size.
prs.matters: Hashing part of many files at once gives the right answer for all of them.

prs.title: rahash2 no longer crashes on empty input
prs.broken: Piping nothing into rahash2 crashed the released version, because it tried to close a file it never opened.
prs.changed: I made it close the file only when one was opened.
prs.matters: Scripts that sometimes pass empty input get a hash instead of a crash.

prs.title: A unit test builds again without network support
prs.broken: When radare2 was built with networking turned off, one of its tests would not compile on newer compilers.
prs.changed: I added the one missing include the test needed.
prs.matters: People building radare2 without networking can run its full test suite.

prs.title: Hashing stops at the end of the file
prs.broken: Asking the hashing tool for a range past the end of a file hashed the last chunk over and over, so the result matched no other tool.
prs.changed: I made the range stop at the file's real size.
prs.matters: A hash of a whole file now matches what standard tools like md5sum print.

prs.title: Block hashes stay inside the range and report read errors
prs.broken: In block mode, the last block could run past the requested end, and a failed read went unnoticed, so the tool hashed stale data.
prs.changed: I made each block stop at the end of the range and made a failed read stop with an error.
prs.matters: Per-block hashes cover exactly the bytes asked for, and a read problem is reported instead of hidden.

prs.title: The number tool reads signed values at the right size
prs.broken: The toolkit's number tool can show a value as a signed number. It guessed the size from the wrong bit, so values like 256 came out as 0 and large numbers came out as -1.
prs.changed: I made it read each value as signed in the smallest of 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits that holds it.
prs.matters: Users converting numbers get the value they typed, not a wrong one.

prs.title: The number tool shows small decimal numbers instead of zero
prs.broken: Converting raw bytes to a decimal number printed only six decimal places, so very small values such as 0.0000001 came out as zero and others lost digits.
prs.changed: The number is now printed with enough digits to get the exact same value back, the way the tool already did for another number format.
prs.matters: People reading values out of a program see what is really stored, not a rounded zero.

prs.title: Changing folders inside the toolkit follows the shell's search list
prs.broken: In a normal terminal, a list of favourite folders lets you jump to a folder by its short name from anywhere. The toolkit's own change-folder command ignored that list, a request open since 2024.
prs.changed: The command now looks the name up in that list the way common shells do, and prints the folder it moved to when the list was used.
prs.matters: People can move around the same way they do in their terminal, including on Windows.

prs.title: Old Mac file dates now print the right year
prs.broken: Old Mac disk formats count time from 1904. The tool added the gap to 1970 instead of taking it away, so every date printed 132 years too late.
prs.changed: The gap is now subtracted, so dates print correctly. The same mistake in a second date printer is fixed as well.
prs.matters: Dates from these disks read correctly.

prs.title: A one byte block no longer crashes a base64 print command
prs.broken: The command that prints a block as base64 reserved too little memory. For a one byte block it wrote two bytes past the end.
prs.changed: The command now uses a helper that reserves the right amount of memory.
prs.matters: A memory error that could crash the tool or be abused is gone.

prs.title: Java byte arrays from the print command now compile
prs.broken: Java bytes run from -128 to 127, but the command printed every byte as 0 to 255. Any byte above 127 gave Java code that would not compile.
prs.changed: Bytes are now printed as signed numbers, such as -112 in place of 144.
prs.matters: The printed Java compiles, and each value still maps back to the same byte.

prs.title: The x86 assembler now builds 64-bit conditional moves correctly
prs.broken: The assembler left out two bytes that mark a 64-bit or extended register. A 64-bit conditional move turned into a 32-bit one and the high registers became the wrong ones.
prs.changed: It now writes those bytes for 16-bit, 64-bit and extended registers, checked against the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Assembled code does what the source says.

prs.title: The x86 assembler now keeps the high registers in basic math
prs.broken: For add, sub, xor, cmp and similar instructions on the extra 64-bit registers in their smaller sizes, the assembler dropped a prefix byte. The instruction quietly used a different, older register instead.
prs.changed: It now writes that byte whenever one of those registers is used, checked against the GNU assembler on 80 cases.
prs.matters: Patching code with these instructions now writes what was typed.

prs.title: The x86 assembler now gets math with memory right
prs.broken: For add, sub, xor, cmp and similar instructions between a register and memory, the assembler wrote the wrong instruction. It mixed up the extra 64-bit registers, dropped part of 32-bit addresses, and refused negative offsets.
prs.changed: These instructions now use the same shared address encoder as mov and lea, checked against the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Patching code with these common instructions now writes what was typed.

prs.title: The x86 assembler learned the bit test instructions
prs.broken: The assembler could not write bt, bts, btr or btc at all. Typing one in any mode just gave "Cannot assemble".
prs.changed: I added all four, on registers and on memory, in 16, 32 and 64-bit code. After review it also rejects bad inputs, like the wrong number of operands. Checked against the GNU assembler on over 4,000 forms.
prs.matters: People patching binaries can now use these instructions instead of typing raw bytes.

prs.title: The x86 assembler writes movzx and movsx correctly
prs.broken: The assembler wrote the wrong bytes for movzx and movsx with most memory operands and some registers. It dropped parts of the address, so the code read from a different place than asked.
prs.changed: These instructions now use the same address encoding as mov and lea, add the prefixes that 16-bit and the newer byte registers need, and reject forms the GNU assembler rejects.
prs.matters: Patches that use these common instructions now do what they say.

prs.title: The arm64 assembler keeps the full number in system call instructions
prs.broken: For system call and breakpoint instructions, the assembler dropped the top bits of the number, so larger values came out wrong, and too-large values were accepted silently.
prs.changed: All 16 bits are now written, and a number that does not fit is rejected.
prs.matters: Patches that use these instructions with larger numbers now do what they say.

prs.title: The x86 assembler now writes not, neg, mul and div correctly
prs.broken: radare2's x86 assembler turned not, neg, mul, div, imul and idiv into the wrong bytes. Byte registers and memory operands came out as a different instruction, and some forms would not assemble at all.
prs.changed: These instructions now pick the right size, register and memory form, and give the same bytes as the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Patching a program with these instructions no longer writes code that does something else.

prs.title: The x86 assembler now accepts the lock prefix
prs.broken: radare2's x86 assembler refused every instruction with the lock prefix, so atomic code like lock inc could not be assembled or patched.
prs.changed: lock now works before the instructions that allow it, with a memory target, and is refused elsewhere, the same as the GNU assembler. The prefix byte goes where GNU puts it.
prs.matters: People patching programs that use atomic operations can now write those instructions in place.

prs.title: The arm64 assembler now writes uxtb and uxth
prs.broken: radare2's arm64 assembler could write the signed sxtb and sxth instructions but refused their unsigned versions, uxtb and uxth.
prs.changed: uxtb and uxth now assemble to the right bytes, and each one reads back as the same text.
prs.matters: Zero-extending a byte or half-word is common in arm64 code, so patches that need it no longer fail.

prs.title: The x86 assembler writes jumps, calls, push and pop correctly
prs.broken: radare2's x86 assembler produced wrong or cut-off bytes for jumps, calls, push, pop, inc and dec when they used memory or newer registers.
prs.changed: These instructions now go through the shared operand code and match the GNU assembler on 186 forms.
prs.matters: Patches that use these common instructions now assemble into code that actually runs.

prs.title: The x86 assembler writes test and xchg with memory correctly
prs.broken: radare2's x86 assembler dropped parts of test and xchg when one side was memory, so the bytes it wrote meant a different instruction.
prs.changed: Both instructions now use the shared memory operand code and give the same bytes as the GNU assembler on over 2,000 forms.
prs.matters: Patches that compare or swap a register with memory now assemble into the code that was asked for.

prs.title: Memory writes with a negative number keep the right address
prs.broken: Assembling an instruction that adds a negative number to a fixed memory address also turned the address negative, so the code wrote somewhere else.
prs.changed: The sign of the number now stays with the number, and the address keeps its own sign.
prs.matters: Patched code touches the memory it was written for.

prs.title: Storing a number into memory assembles correctly
prs.broken: Putting a number straight into memory came out as a different instruction for several kinds of address, with no error.
prs.changed: These now assemble to the same bytes as the GNU assembler, and bad sizes give an error.
prs.matters: Patches that store values in memory do what they say.

prs.title: The test instruction keeps its memory offset
prs.broken: Testing bits at a memory address dropped the offset and some register bits, so it checked the wrong place.
prs.changed: The instruction now keeps the offset, the index register and the number's sign.
prs.matters: Patched checks look at the memory they name.

prs.title: Addresses that start with a minus sign are no longer off by one
prs.broken: A memory address written with a leading minus, like [-8] or [ebp+-8], came out one byte too far.
prs.changed: The minus sign is now read as part of the number.
prs.matters: Code that reads local variables below the frame pointer reaches the right ones.

prs.title: 64-bit moves to a fixed address assemble correctly
prs.broken: In 64-bit code, moving a register to or from a fixed address quietly became a different instruction.
prs.changed: These now use the same encodings as the GNU assembler, including the short form for the main register.
prs.matters: Patches in 64-bit programs that read or write fixed addresses work.

prs.title: Bytes changed in memory are colored in hex and disassembly views
prs.broken: After writing bytes in a session without saving them to the file, nothing in the hex or code views showed which bytes were changed.
prs.changed: Those bytes now show in the diff color in the hex dump and in the byte column of the disassembly.
prs.matters: People patching a binary can see their edits at a glance before saving them.

prs.title: Segment overrides on memory operands assemble correctly
prs.broken: Instructions that read through fs: or gs:, like the stack canary load, lost their address and came out as a different instruction, or failed to assemble.
prs.changed: The segment prefix is now placed first and the address is encoded as a normal memory operand, matching the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Patching code that touches thread-local data or the stack guard now gives the right bytes.

prs.title: xadd assembles with the right sizes and memory targets
prs.broken: xadd only worked between two registers, and in 64-bit code every form was widened to 64 bits, so most came out as a different instruction.
prs.changed: It now picks the operand size, extended registers and memory targets from the operands, matching the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Atomic add instructions, common in lock-free code, now assemble to the right bytes.

prs.title: test between two registers assembles to the right bytes
prs.broken: test between two registers only came out right for two 64-bit ones. Other pairs, like r8 with rax or two 16-bit registers, became a different instruction.
prs.changed: Each register pair now gets the prefixes it needs, matching the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: A common compare instruction now assembles correctly for every register size.

prs.title: setcc assembles to the right bytes for new registers and memory
prs.broken: setcc lost its prefix, so sete r9b became sete cl. Memory forms with an offset, like a local variable, came out cut short.
prs.changed: setcc now gets the prefix it needs and writes the full memory operand, matching the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Setting a byte from a comparison now assembles correctly for every register and memory form.

prs.title: Conditional moves from memory assemble to the right bytes
prs.broken: cmov instructions that read from memory came out wrong for common forms, like a stack offset, a fixed address, or a newer register as the base.
prs.changed: The memory operand is now encoded the same way as for other instructions, matching the GNU assembler.
prs.matters: Conditional moves, used everywhere in compiled code, now assemble correctly when they read memory.

prs.title: 8 and 16-bit register moves assemble to the right registers
prs.broken: Moving between 8 or 16-bit registers that need an extra prefix, like r10w or sil, silently became a move between two different registers.
prs.changed: These moves now get the prefixes they need, and invalid register pairs are rejected like the GNU assembler does.
prs.matters: mov is the most common instruction, so small register moves now assemble to what was written.
